mishnayos.summary: This mishnah asks when we may start saying Shema at night, and until when. The Rabbis also teach that they set an early deadline to keep people from missing the mitzvah.

chunks.en: From what time do we say Shema at night?
From the time the Kohanim go in to eat their terumah,

words.note: Kohanim are the family of Aharon who served in the Beis HaMikdash.
Terumah is a special gift of food given to Kohanim; they may eat it only when they are pure, after nightfall.

chunks.en: until the end of the first part of the night.

words.note: The night was split into three or four "watches," like shifts of guards.

chunks.en: These are the words of Rabbi Eliezer.

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: But the Sages say,
until midnight.
Rabban Gamliel says,

words.note: A title for the leader of the Jewish people.
A great Rabbi of the Mishnah, head of the Sanhedrin.

chunks.en: until the first light of dawn comes up.

words.note: The first light that shows in the sky before sunrise.

chunks.en: Once his sons came home from a wedding party.
They said to him,
"We did not say Shema yet."
He said to them,
"If dawn has not come up yet,
you still must say it.
And not only this,
but everything that the Sages said
must be done by midnight,
may really be done until dawn.
Burning the fats and limbs of korbanos

words.note: Special fat parts of a korban that were burned on the mizbeach.
Parts of a korban burned whole on the mizbeach.

chunks.en: may be done until dawn.
And all korbanos that are eaten for just one day
may be eaten until dawn.
If so,
why did the Sages say "until midnight"?

chunks.he: כְּדֵי לְהַרְחִיק אֶת הָאָדָם מִן הָעֲבֵרָה:
chunks.en: To keep a person far away from sinning.

mishnayos.english: The beginning of tractate Berakhot, the first tractate in the first of the six orders of Mishna, opens with a discussion of the recitation of Shema, as the recitation of Shema encompasses an acceptance of the yoke of Heaven and of the mitzvot, and as such, forms the basis for all subsequent teachings. The Mishna opens with the laws regarding the appropriate time to recite Shema: From when, that is, from what time, does one recite Shema in the evening? From the time when the priests enter to partake of their teruma. Until when does the time for the recitation of the evening Shema extend? Until the end of the first watch. The term used in the Torah (Deuteronomy 6:7) to indicate the time for the recitation of the evening Shema is beshokhbekha, when you lie down, which refers to the time in which individuals go to sleep. Therefore, the time for the recitation of Shema is the first portion of the night, when individuals typically prepare for sleep. That is the statement of Rabbi Eliezer. The Rabbis say: The time for the recitation of the evening Shema is until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says: One may recite Shema until dawn, indicating that beshokhbekha is to be understood as a reference to the entire time people sleep in their beds, the whole night. The mishna relates that Rabban Gamliel practiced in accordance with his ruling. There was an incident where Rabban Gamliel’s sons returned very late from a wedding hall. They said to him, as they had been preoccupied with celebrating with the groom and bride: We did not recite Shema. He said to them: If the dawn has not yet arrived, you are obligated to recite Shema. Since Rabban Gamliel’s opinion disagreed with that of the Rabbis, he explained to his sons that the Rabbis actually agree with him, and that it is not only with regard to the halakha of the recitation of Shema, but rather, wherever the Sages say until midnight, the mitzva may be performed until dawn. Rabban Gamliel cites several cases in support of his claim, such as the burning of fats and limbs on the altar. Due to the quantity of offerings each day, the priests were often unable to complete the burning of all of the fats and limbs, so they continued to be burned into the night, as it is written: “This is the law of the burnt offering: The burnt offering shall remain upon the pyre on the altar all night until morning, while the fire on the altar burns it” (Leviticus 6:2). And, with regard to all sacrifices, such as the sin-offerings and the guilt-offerings that are eaten for one day and night; although the Sages state that they may be eaten only until midnight, by Torah law they may be eaten until dawn. This is in accordance with the verse: “On the day on which it is offered must you eat. Do not leave it until the morning” (Leviticus 7:15). If so, why did the Sages say that they may be eaten only until midnight? This is in order to distance a person from transgression, as if one believes that he has until dawn to perform the mitzva, he might be negligent and postpone it until the opportunity to perform the mitzva has passed.

mishnayos.summary: This mishnah teaches when we may start saying Shema in the morning, and until when.

chunks.en: From what time do we say Shema in the morning?
From when one can tell blue from white.

words.note: Techeiles is the special blue color used in tzitzis.

chunks.en: Rabbi Eliezer says,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: between blue and leek-green.

words.note: A leek is a green vegetable whose color is close to blue.

chunks.en: And one must finish it by sunrise.
Rabbi Yehoshua says,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: until three hours into the day,
because that is the way of princes,
to get up at three hours.
Someone who says it later did not lose out;
he is like a person learning Torah.

mishnayos.english: From when does one recite Shema in the morning? From when a person can distinguish between sky-blue [tekhelet] and white. Rabbi Eliezer says: From when one can distinguish between sky-blue and leek-green. And one must finish reciting Shema until the end of the period when you rise, i.e., sunrise, when the sun begins to shine. Rabbi Yehoshua says: One may recite the morning Shema until three hours of the day, which this is still considered when you rise, as that is the habit of kings to rise from their sleep at three hours of the day. While there is a set time frame for the recitation of Shema, one who recites Shema from that time onward loses nothing. Although he does not fulfill the mitzva of reciting of Shema at its appointed time, he is nevertheless considered like one who reads the Torah, and is rewarded accordingly.

mishnayos.summary: Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel argue about whether we must lie down at night and stand in the morning to say Shema. The halacha follows Beis Hillel: say it however you are.

chunks.en: Beis Shammai say,

words.note: Beis Shammai were the students of Shammai, a great early Sage.

chunks.en: at night everyone should lean over and read,
and in the morning they should stand,
as it says, "when you lie down and when you get up."
And Beis Hillel say,

words.note: Beis Hillel were the students of Hillel, a great early Sage.

chunks.en: everyone reads in his own way,
as it says, "and when you walk on the road."
If so,
why does it say "when you lie down and when you get up"?
It means at the time people go to sleep,
and at the time people get up.
Rabbi Tarfon said,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: "I was traveling on the road,
and I lay down to read,
like Beis Shammai say,
and I put myself in danger from robbers."
They said to him,
"You deserved to be punished,
because you went against Beis Hillel."

mishnayos.english: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disputed the proper way to recite Shema. Beit Shammai say: One should recite Shema in the manner indicated in the text of Shema itself. Therefore, in the evening every person must recline on his side and recite Shema, in fulfillment of the verse: “When you lie down,” and in the morning he must stand and recite Shema, in fulfillment of the verse: When you rise, as it is stated: “When you lie down, and when you rise.” And Beit Hillel say: Every person recites Shema as he is, and he may do so in whatever position is most comfortable for him, both day and night, as it is stated: “And when you walk along the way,” when one is neither standing nor reclining (Me’iri). If so, according to Beit Hillel, why was it stated: “When you lie down, and when you rise”? This is merely to denote time; at the time when people lie down and the time when people rise. With regard to this halakha, Rabbi Tarfon said: Once, I was coming on the road when I stopped and reclined to recite Shema in accordance with the statement of Beit Shammai. Although Rabbi Tarfon was a disciple of Beit Hillel, he thought that fulfilling the mitzva in accordance with the opinion of Beit Shammai would be a more meticulous fulfillment of the mitzva, acceptable to all opinions. Yet in so doing, I endangered myself due to the highwaymen [listim] who accost travelers. The Sages said to him: You deserved to be in a position where you were liable to pay with your life, as you transgressed the statement of Beit Hillel. This statement will be explained in the Gemara.

mishnayos.summary: This mishnah tells how many brachos we say before and after Shema, and that we must not change the way the Sages wrote each bracha.

chunks.he: בַּשַּׁחַר מְבָרֵךְ שְׁתַּיִם לְפָנֶיהָ וְאַחַת לְאַחֲרֶיהָ,
chunks.en: In the morning one says two brachos before it and one after it,
and at night two before it and two after it.
One long and one short.
Where the Sages said to make it long,
one may not make it short.
Where they said to make it short, one may not make it long.
Where they said to end with "Baruch," one may not skip it.

words.note: Closing a bracha means ending it with "Baruch Atah Hashem..."

chunks.en: And where they said not to end that way,
one may not add an ending.

mishnayos.english: From the laws of the recitation of Shema itself, the mishna proceeds to discuss the blessings recited in conjunction with Shema. Here, the order is established: In the morning when reciting Shema, one recites two blessings beforehand, the first on the radiant lights and the second the blessing on the love of Torah, and one thereafter, which begins with: True and Firm [emet veyatziv]. And in the evening one recites two blessings beforehand, on the radiant lights and on the love of God, and two thereafter, the blessing of redemption: True and Faithful [emet ve’emuna], and the blessing: Help us lie down. With regard to the blessing: True and Faithful, whether one recites it in its long formula and whether one recites it in its short formula, he fulfills his obligation (Tosafot). However, the general principle is: Where the Sages said to recite a long blessing, one may not shorten it, and so too, wherever they said to recite a short blessing, one may not lengthen it. Where the Sages said that a blessing must conclude with a second blessing at the end, he may not fail to conclude with that blessing. Similarly, if the Sages said that a blessing must not conclude with a second blessing, one may not conclude with a blessing.

mishnayos.summary: We remember leaving Egypt every night too, in the last part of Shema. Ben Zoma learned this from a pasuk, and the Sages learned that we will remember it even in the days of Mashiach.

chunks.en: We mention leaving Egypt at night.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah said,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah who became head of the Sanhedrin when he was very young.

chunks.en: "I am like a seventy-year-old man,

chunks.he: וְלֹא זָכִיתִי שֶׁתֵּאָמֵר יְצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם בַּלֵּילוֹת,
chunks.en: and I could not prove that leaving Egypt must be said at night,
until Ben Zoma explained it,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah, famous for explaining pesukim.

chunks.en: as it says, "So that you will remember
the day you left the land of Egypt
all the days of your life."
"The days of your life" means
the days. "All the days of your life"
adds the nights. But the Sages say,
"The days of your life" means
this world.
"All the days of your life"
adds the days of Mashiach.

mishnayos.english: It is a mitzva by Torah law to mention the exodus from Egypt at night, but some held that this mitzva was, like phylacteries or ritual fringes, fulfilled only during the day and not at night. For this reason it was decided: The exodus from Egypt is mentioned at night, adjacent to the recitation of Shema. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya said: I am approximately seventy years old, and although I have long held this opinion, I was never privileged to prevail (Me’iri) and prove that there is a biblical obligation to fulfill the accepted custom (Ra’avad) and have the exodus from Egypt mentioned at night, until Ben Zoma interpreted it homiletically and proved it obligatory. Ben Zoma derived it as it is stated: “That you may remember the day you went out of the land of Egypt all the days of your life” (Deuteronomy 16:3). The days of your life, refers to daytime alone; however, the addition of the word all, as it is stated: All the days of your life, comes to add nights as well. And the Rabbis, who posit that there is no biblical obligation to mention the exodus from Egypt at night, explain the word, all, differently and say: The days of your life, refers to the days in this world, all is added to include the days of the Messiah.

mishnayos.summary: To do the mitzvah of Shema you must have in mind to do it. This mishnah also teaches when you may stop in the middle of Shema to greet someone.

chunks.en: If someone was reading the Torah
and the time came to say Shema,
if he had in mind to do the mitzvah,
he did the mitzvah. And if not,
he did not do the mitzvah.
Between the sections, he may greet someone out of respect, and answer,
and in the middle, he may greet someone he fears, and answer.

words.note: Someone he is afraid of, like a king or a dangerous person.

chunks.en: These are the words of Rabbi Meir.

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehudah says,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: in the middle he may greet someone he fears,
and answer someone he respects;
between the sections he may greet someone he respects,
and answer "Shalom" to anyone.

mishnayos.english: The first question discussed in the mishna is the question of intent. One who was reading the sections of the Torah which comprise Shema, and the time for the recitation of the morning or evening Shema arrived, if he focused his heart, he fulfilled his obligation and need not repeat Shema in order to fulfill his obligation. This is true even if he failed to recite the requisite blessings (Rabbeinu Ḥananel). Ab initio, one may not interrupt the recitation of Shema. The tanna’im, however, disagree over how strict one must be in this regard. They distinguish between interruptions between paragraphs and interruptions within each paragraph. At the breaks between paragraphs, one may greet an individual due to the respect that he is obligated to show him, and one may respond to another’s greeting due to respect. And in the middle of each paragraph one may greet an individual due to the fear that the individual may harm him if he fails do so (Me’iri) and one may respond to another’s greeting due to fear. This is the statement of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says: There is a distinction between greeting someone and responding to his greeting. In the middle of each paragraph, one may greet another due to fear and respond due to respect. In the breaks between paragraphs, one may greet another due to respect and respond with a greeting to any person who greets him, whether or not he is obligated to show him respect.

mishnayos.summary: This mishnah lists the places "between the sections" of Shema and its brachos, and explains why the parts of Shema are in their order.

chunks.en: These are the places "between the sections":
between the first bracha and the second,
between the second and Shema,
and between Shema and "Vehayah im shamoa,"

words.note: The second paragraph of Shema.

chunks.en: between "Vehayah im shamoa" and "Vayomer,"

words.note: The third paragraph of Shema, about tzitzis.

chunks.en: between "Vayomer" and "Emes Veyatziv."

words.note: The bracha right after Shema in the morning.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehudah says,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.he: בֵּין וַיֹּאמֶר לֶאֱמֶת וְיַצִּיב לֹא יַפְסִיק.
chunks.en: between "Vayomer" and "Emes Veyatziv" one may not stop.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korchah said,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.he: לָמָּה קָדְמָה שְׁמַע לִוְהָיָה אִם שָׁמֹעַ,
chunks.en: Why does Shema come before "Vehayah im shamoa"?
So that a person first accepts
Hashem as his King,

words.note: Accepting Hashem as our King.

chunks.he: וְאַחַר כָּךְ יְקַבֵּל עָלָיו עֹל מִצְוֹת.
chunks.en: and after that he accepts the mitzvos.
And "Vehayah im shamoa" comes before "Vayomer,"

chunks.he: שֶׁוְהָיָה אִם שָׁמֹעַ נוֹהֵג בַּיּוֹם וּבַלַּיְלָה,
chunks.en: because "Vehayah im shamoa" applies day and night,
but "Vayomer" only applies in the daytime.

words.note: Because it is about tzitzis, which we wear in the daytime.

mishnayos.english: As for what constitutes a paragraph, these are the breaks between the paragraphs: Between the first blessing and the second, between the second and Shema, between Shema and the second paragraph: If you indeed heed My commandments [VeHaya im Shamoa], between VeHaya im Shamoa and the third paragraph: And the Lord spoke [VaYomer] and between VaYomer and True and Firm [emet veyatziv], the blessing that follows Shema. The Rabbis held that each blessing and each paragraph of Shema constitutes its own entity, and treat interruptions between them as between the paragraphs. Rabbi Yehuda, however, says: Between VaYomer and emet veyatziv, which begins the blessing that follows Shema, one may not interrupt at all. According to Rabbi Yehuda, these must be recited consecutively. Since the paragraphs of Shema are not adjacent to one another in the Torah, and they are not recited in the order in which they appear, the mishna explains their placement. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa said: Why, in the mitzva of the recitation of Shema, did the portion of Shema precede that of VeHaya im Shamoa? This is so that one will first accept upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, the awareness of God and God’s unity, and only then accept upon himself the yoke of the mitzvot, which appears in the paragraph of VeHaya im Shamoa. Why did VeHaya im Shamoa precede VaYomer? Because the paragraph of VeHaya im Shamoa is practiced both by day and by night, while VaYomer, which discusses the mitzva of ritual fringes, is only practiced during the day.

mishnayos.summary: This mishnah teaches what happens if you say Shema too quietly, unclearly, out of order, or with a mistake.

chunks.he: הַקּוֹרֵא אֶת שְׁמַע וְלֹא הִשְׁמִיעַ לְאָזְנוֹ,
chunks.en: If someone says Shema so quietly that his own ears cannot hear it,
he did the mitzvah. Rabbi Yosi says,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: he did not do the mitzvah.
If he read without saying each letter carefully,
Rabbi Yosi says he did the mitzvah,
Rabbi Yehudah says he did not.

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: If someone reads it out of order,
he did not do the mitzvah.
If he read and made a mistake,
he goes back to the place of the mistake.

mishnayos.english: One who recites Shema and did not recite in a manner audible to his own ear, either because he read inaudibly or because he is deaf, fulfilled his obligation. Rabbi Yosei says: He did not fulfill his obligation. One who recited Shema and was not sufficiently precise in his enunciation of its letters, Rabbi Yosei says: He fulfilled his obligation. Rabbi Yehuda says: He did not fulfill his obligation. One who recited Shema out of order, meaning he did not read the verses sequentially, he did not fulfill his obligation. One who recited and erred, should return to the place in Shema that he erred.

mishnayos.summary: Workers may say Shema while up in a tree or on a wall, but they must come down to daven Shemoneh Esrei.

chunks.en: Workers may say Shema at the top of a tree
or at the top of a row of stones in a wall,

words.note: A row of stones in a wall that is being built.

chunks.he: מַה שֶּׁאֵינָן רַשָּׁאִין לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן בַּתְּפִלָּה:
chunks.en: which they may not do for davening Shemoneh Esrei.

words.note: Here "tefillah" means Shemoneh Esrei.

mishnayos.english: The primary issue in this mishna is the requisite degree of concentration when reciting Shema. Laborers engaged in their work may recite Shema while standing atop the tree or atop the course of stones in a wall under construction, which they are not permitted to do for the Amida prayer, which requires intent of the heart.

mishnayos.summary: A chassan does not have to say Shema on his wedding night, because he is too busy thinking. But Rabban Gamliel said it anyway, because he did not want to stop accepting Hashem as King even for a moment.

chunks.en: A chassan does not have to say Shema on the night

words.note: A chassan is a groom who just got married.

chunks.en: the first, until after Shabbos,
if he has not yet done the act of marriage.
There was a story with Rabban Gamliel, who said Shema

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah, head of the Sanhedrin.

chunks.en: on the first night after he got married.
His students said to him,
"Didn't you teach us,

chunks.he: רַבֵּנוּ, שֶׁחָתָן פָּטוּר מִקְּרִיאַת שְׁמַע בַּלַּיְלָה הָרִאשׁוֹן.
chunks.en: our Rebbi, that a chassan does not have to say Shema on the first night?"
He said to them,
"I will not listen to you and take off from myself
Hashem as my King, even for one hour."

words.note: Accepting Hashem as our King.

mishnayos.english: The mishna continues: A groom is exempt from the recitation of Shema on the first night of his marriage, which was generally Wednesday night, until Saturday night, if he has not taken action and consummated the marriage, as he is preoccupied by concerns related to consummation of the marriage. The mishna relates that there was an incident where Rabban Gamliel married a woman and recited Shema even the first night. His students said to him: Didn’t our teacher teach us that a groom is exempt from the recitation of Shema? He answered them: Nevertheless, I am not listening to you to refrain from reciting Shema, and in so doing preclude myself from the acceptance of the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, for even one moment.

mishnayos.summary: Rabban Gamliel washed himself on the first night after his wife died, even though a mourner may not wash. He explained that he was a very delicate person who would get sick without washing.

chunks.en: He washed on the first night after his wife died.
His students said to him,
"Didn't you teach us,
our Rebbi, that a mourner may not wash?"

words.note: An avel is someone whose close relative just died.

chunks.en: He said to them,
"I am not like all other people,
I am very delicate."

words.note: Someone so sensitive that not washing would make him sick.

mishnayos.english: The mishna relates another episode portraying unusual conduct by Rabban Gamliel. He bathed on the first night after his wife died. His students said to him: Have you not taught us, our teacher, that a mourner is prohibited to bathe? He answered them: I am not like other people, I am delicate [istenis]. For me, not bathing causes actual physical distress, and even a mourner need not suffer physical distress as part of his mourning.

mishnayos.summary: When Rabban Gamliel's servant Tavi died, he accepted comforting like for a family member. He explained that Tavi was a very special, righteous servant.

chunks.en: And when Tavi, his servant, died,
he let people come comfort him.

words.note: Words of comfort said to a mourner.

chunks.en: His students said to him,
"Didn't you teach us, our Rebbi,
that we do not accept comforting for servants?"
He said to them,

chunks.he: אֵין טָבִי עַבְדִּי כִּשְׁאָר כָּל הָעֲבָדִים,
chunks.en: "My servant Tavi is not like all other servants;
he was a good and proper man."

mishnayos.english: Another exceptional incident is related: And when his slave, Tavi, died, Rabban Gamliel accepted condolences for his death as one would for a close family member. His students said to him: Have you not taught us, our teacher, that one does not accept condolences for the death of slaves? Rabban Gamliel said to his students: My slave, Tavi, is not like all the rest of the slaves, he was virtuous and it is appropriate to accord him the same respect accorded to a family member.

mishnayos.summary: A chassan may say Shema on his first night if he wants. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says not everyone should act as if he is so holy that he can concentrate.

chunks.en: A chassan, if he wants to say

words.note: A groom who just got married.

chunks.en: Shema on the first night,

chunks.he: קוֹרֵא. רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר,
chunks.en: may say it. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah, head of the Sanhedrin.

chunks.en: not everyone who wants to take
the name may take it.

words.note: Here it means a name for being extra holy.

mishnayos.english: With regard to the recitation of Shema on one’s wedding night, the Sages said that if, despite his exemption, a groom wishes to recite Shema on the first night, he may do so. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: Not everyone who wishes to assume the reputation of a God-fearing person may assume it, and consequently, not everyone who wishes to recite Shema on his wedding night may do so.

mishnayos.summary: Someone whose close relative just died and is not yet buried is too busy to say Shema, daven, or put on tefillin. The people carrying the coffin also don't say Shema if they are needed.

chunks.en: Someone whose dead relative is lying in front of him, not yet buried,
does not have to say Shema,
or daven Shemoneh Esrei, or put on tefillin.

words.note: The main prayer we say standing, also called the Amidah.

chunks.en: The people who carry the coffin, the ones who take their place, and the ones who take their place after that,

words.note: The bed or stretcher the person who died is carried on.

chunks.he: אֶת שֶׁלִּפְנֵי הַמִּטָּה וְאֶת שֶׁלְּאַחַר הַמִּטָּה,
chunks.en: both those walking in front of the coffin and those behind it,
the ones who are needed to carry it do not have to say Shema,

chunks.he: וְאֶת שֶׁאֵין לַמִּטָּה צֹרֶךְ בָּהֶן חַיָּבִין.
chunks.en: but the ones who are not needed to carry it must say Shema.
Both groups do not have to daven Shemoneh Esrei.

mishnayos.english: One whose deceased relative is laid out unburied before him is exempt from the recitation of Shema, from the Amida prayer, and from the mitzva to don phylacteries, until the deceased has been buried. With regard to the pallbearers and their replacements and the replacements of their replacements, those located before the bier who have not yet carried the deceased and those located after the bier. Those who are needed to carry the bier are exempt from reciting Shema; while those who are not needed to carry the bier, are obligated to recite Shema. However, both these and those are exempt from reciting the Amida prayer, since they are preoccupied and are unable to focus and pray with the appropriate intent.

mishnayos.summary: After a funeral, people may start Shema only if they can finish before they reach the line of people comforting the mourners. In that line, only the people in the front row are free from saying Shema.

chunks.en: If they buried the person who died and came back,
if they can start and finish saying Shema
before they get to the line,

words.note: After a burial, people stand in rows so the mourners can walk between them and be comforted.

chunks.en: they should start.
But if not, they should not start.
Of the people standing in the line,
the ones in the inside row do not have to say Shema,

words.note: The ones right next to the mourners, who comfort them.

chunks.en: but the ones in the outside row must say it.

mishnayos.english: After they buried the deceased and returned, if they have sufficient time to begin to recite Shema and conclude before they arrive at the row, formed by those who attended the burial, through which the bereaved family will pass in order to receive consolation, they should begin. If they do not have sufficient time to conclude reciting the entire Shema, then they should not begin. And those standing in the row, those in the interior row, directly before whom the mourners will pass and who will console them, are exempt from reciting Shema, while those in the exterior row, who stand there only to show their respect, are obligated to recite Shema.

mishnayos.summary: Women, slaves, and children don't have to say Shema or wear tefillin. But they do have to daven, have a mezuzah, and bentch after eating.

chunks.en: Women, slaves, and children do not have to

words.note: Servants who belonged to a Jewish master and kept some mitzvos.

chunks.en: say Shema or put on tefillin,
but they must daven and have a mezuzah,
and bentch after eating bread.

words.note: Bentching, the bracha said after eating bread.

mishnayos.english: Women, slaves and minors are exempt from the recitation of Shema and from phylacteries, but are obligated in prayer, mezuza and Grace after Meals.

mishnayos.summary: A man who is tamei from a certain kind of impurity may only think the Shema in his heart without saying the brachos. After food he says the bracha, but not before it. Rabbi Yehuda says he says the brachos before and after.

chunks.he: בַּעַל קֶרִי מְהַרְהֵר בְּלִבּוֹ וְאֵינוֹ מְבָרֵךְ,
chunks.en: A man who is tamei in a certain way thinks the Shema in his heart and does not say the brachos,

words.note: A kind of impurity from the body; he must go to the mikvah before learning Torah.

chunks.en: not before it and not after it.
And for food, he says the bracha after eating,
but he does not say the bracha before eating.
Rabbi Yehuda says,

words.note: Rabbi Yehuda was a great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: he says the brachos before them and after them.

mishnayos.english: Ezra the Scribe decreed that one who is ritually impure because of a seminal emission may not engage in matters of Torah until he has immersed in a ritual bath and purified himself. This halakha was accepted over the course of many generations; however, many disputes arose with regard to the Torah matters to which it applies. Regarding this, the mishna says: If the time for the recitation of Shema arrived and one is impure due to a seminal emission, he may contemplate Shema in his heart, but neither recites the blessings preceding Shema, nor the blessings following it. Over food which, after partaking, one is obligated by Torah law to recite a blessing, one recites a blessing afterward, but one does not recite a blessing beforehand, because the blessing recited prior to eating is a requirement by rabbinic law. And in all of these instances Rabbi Yehuda says: He recites a blessing beforehand and thereafter in both the case of Shema and in the case of food.

mishnayos.summary: If a man remembers in the middle of davening that he is tamei, he makes his davening shorter. If he went to the mikvah in the morning, he must cover himself before saying Shema, and stay away from dirty water and from a bad smell.

chunks.en: If a man was standing and davening,
and he remembered that he is tamei,

words.note: A kind of impurity from the body; he must go to the mikvah.

chunks.en: he should not stop,
but he should make it shorter.
If he went down into the mikvah to dip,

words.note: To go under the water of a mikvah to become tahor.

chunks.en: if he can come up, get dressed, and say Shema
before the sun comes up,
he should come up, get dressed, and say it.
And if not,
he should cover himself with the water and say it there.
But he should not cover himself

chunks.he: לֹא בַמַּיִם הָרָעִים וְלֹא בְמֵי הַמִּשְׁרָה,
chunks.en: not in smelly water and not in water where flax was soaking,

words.note: Water where flax plants were soaked, which smells bad.

chunks.en: until he pours fresh water into it.
And how far must he stay away from them and from a dirty mess?
Four amos.

words.note: An amah is about the length of a grown-up's arm, about 2 feet.

mishnayos.english: This mishna contains various statements with regard to individuals with different types of ritual impurity as well as the need to distance oneself from filth and impurity. One who was standing in prayer and he recalled that he experienced a seminal emission, and according to this opinion he is prohibited from praying, should not interrupt his prayer, rather he should abridge each individual blessing. They stated a general principle: One who descended to immerse himself, if he is able to ascend, cover himself with a garment, and recite the morning Shema before sunrise, he should ascend, cover himself, and recite Shema, and if not, he should cover himself in the water and recite Shema there. He may not, however, cover himself in either foul water, or water in which flax was soaked, until he pours other water into it. And in general, how far must one distance himself from urine and feces in order to recite Shema? At least four cubits.

mishnayos.summary: Some people who are already tamei in a bigger way also became tamei in a smaller way. The Chachamim say they still need to go to the mikvah before davening and learning, but Rabbi Yehuda says they don't.

chunks.en: A zav who also became tamei from a seminal emission,

words.note: A man who is tamei for at least seven days because of an illness.
Another kind of impurity from the body.

chunks.en: and a niddah who also became tamei in another way,

words.note: A woman who is tamei for at least seven days at certain times of the month.

chunks.en: and a married woman who became a niddah,

words.en: and a woman with her husband

chunks.en: all need to go to the mikvah.
But Rabbi Yehuda says they don't have to.

words.note: Rabbi Yehuda was a great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

mishnayos.english: Continuing the earlier discussion of the halakhot of immersion for Torah study and prayer for one who experienced a seminal emission, the mishna discusses a case where individuals who were already impure with a severe form of ritual impurity are exposed to the impurity of a seminal emission as well. They are required to immerse themselves and purify themselves of the impurity of the seminal emission even though they remain impure due to the more severe impurity. Consequently, even a zav, whose impurity lasts at least seven days, who experienced a seminal emission, for which, were he not a zav, he would be impure for only one day; a menstruating woman who discharged semen, despite the fact that she is already impure with a severe impurity unaffected by her immersion; and a woman who engaged in conjugal relations with her husband and later saw menstrual blood, all require immersion. And Rabbi Yehuda exempts them from immersion.

mishnayos.summary: This mishnah tells us until what time we may daven each tefillah: Shacharis, Mincha, Maariv, and Musaf.

chunks.en: The morning tefillah, Shacharis, may be said until midday.
Rabbi Yehuda says,

words.note: Rabbi Yehuda was a great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: until four hours into the day.

words.note: Hours counted from sunrise, about a third of the day.

chunks.en: The tefillah of Mincha may be said until evening.
Rabbi Yehuda says,

words.note: Rabbi Yehuda was a great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: until the middle of the afternoon.

words.note: Plag haMincha, a little over an hour before nightfall.

chunks.en: The evening tefillah, Maariv, has no set time.
And Musaf may be said all day.

words.note: The extra tefillah on Shabbos, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehuda says,

words.note: Rabbi Yehuda was a great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: until seven hours into the day.

mishnayos.english: This mishna determines the times beyond which the different prayers may not be recited. According to the Rabbis, the morning prayer may be recited until noon. Rabbi Yehuda says: It may be recited only until four hours after sunrise. According to the Rabbis, the afternoon prayer may be recited until the evening. Rabbi Yehuda says: It may be recited only until the midpoint of the afternoon [pelag haminḥa], i.e., the midpoint of the period that begins with the sacrifice of the daily afternoon offering and ends at nightfall, which is the end of the afternoon. The evening prayer may be recited throughout the night and is not fixed to a specific hour. According to the Rabbis, the additional prayer may be recited all day. Rabbi Yehuda says: It may be recited only until seven hours after sunrise.

mishnayos.summary: Rabbi Nechunya ben Hakanah said a short tefillah when he went into the beis midrash and when he left. Going in, he asked not to make any mistakes, and going out, he thanked Hashem for his share in learning.

chunks.he: רַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא בֶּן הַקָּנָה הָיָה מִתְפַּלֵּל
chunks.en: Rabbi Nechunya ben Hakanah used to daven

words.note: Rabbi Nechunya ben Hakanah was a great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.he: בִּכְנִיסָתוֹ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ וּבִיצִיאָתוֹ תְּפִלָּה קְצָרָה.
chunks.en: a short tefillah when he went into the beis midrash and when he left it.

words.note: The beis midrash, where people learn Torah.

chunks.en: They asked him,
what is this tefillah for?
He told them,
When I go in, I daven
that no mistake should happen because of me,

chunks.he: וּבִיצִיאָתִי אֲנִי נוֹתֵן הוֹדָיָה עַל חֶלְקִי:
chunks.en: and when I go out, I thank Hashem for my share.

mishnayos.english: In addition to the halakhot relating to the fixed prayers, the Gemara relates: Rabbi Neḥunya ben Hakana would recite a brief prayer upon his entrance into the study hall and upon his exit. They said to him: The study hall is not a dangerous place that would warrant a prayer when entering and exiting, so what room is there for this prayer? He said to them: Upon my entrance, I pray that no mishap will transpire caused by me in the study hall. And upon my exit, I give thanks for my portion.

mishnayos.summary: Rabban Gamliel says we must say all of Shemoneh Esrei every day. Rabbi Yehoshua says a short version is enough, and Rabbi Akiva says it depends on whether the person knows it well.

chunks.en: Rabban Gamliel says,

words.note: Rabban Gamliel was the leader of the Jewish people in the time of the Mishnah.

chunks.he: בְּכָל יוֹם מִתְפַּלֵּל אָדָם שְׁמֹנֶה עֶשְׂרֵה.
chunks.en: every day a person davens Shemoneh Esrei.

words.note: Shemoneh Esrei, the tefillah of eighteen brachos.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehoshua says,

words.note: Rabbi Yehoshua was a great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: a short version of Shemoneh Esrei.
Rabbi Akiva says,

words.note: Rabbi Akiva was a great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: if he knows his tefillah smoothly by heart,
he should daven all of Shemoneh Esrei.
And if not,
a short version of Shemoneh Esrei.

mishnayos.english: The mishna cites a dispute with regard to the obligation to recite the Amida prayer, also known as Shemoneh Esreh, the prayer of eighteen blessings, or simply as tefilla, prayer. Rabban Gamliel says: Each and every day a person recites the prayer of eighteen blessings. Rabbi Yehoshua says: A short prayer is sufficient, and one only recites an abridged version of the prayer of eighteen blessings. Rabbi Akiva says an intermediate opinion: If he is fluent in his prayer, he recites the prayer of eighteen blessings, and if not, he need only recite an abridged version of the prayer of eighteen blessings.

mishnayos.summary: Rabbi Eliezer teaches that davening must not be like a chore, but should be asking Hashem from the heart. Rabbi Yehoshua gives a short tefillah for someone traveling in a dangerous place.

chunks.en: Rabbi Eliezer says,

words.note: Rabbi Eliezer was a great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: someone who makes his davening like a fixed chore,
his davening is not real begging for mercy.
Rabbi Yehoshua says,

words.note: Rabbi Yehoshua was a great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: someone who is walking in a dangerous place
says a short tefillah.
He says: Hashem, save Your people,
the ones left of the Jewish people.

chunks.he: בְּכָל פָּרָשַׁת הָעִבּוּר יִהְיוּ צָרְכֵיהֶם לְפָנֶיךָ.
chunks.en: At every hard time, may their needs be in front of You.

words.note: A time of trouble or change; the Gemara explains this phrase.

chunks.en: Blessed are You, Hashem, Who hears tefillah.

mishnayos.english: Rabbi Eliezer says: One whose prayer is fixed, his prayer is not supplication and is flawed. The Gemara will clarify the halakhic implications of this flaw. Rabbi Yehoshua says: One who cannot recite a complete prayer because he is walking in a place of danger, recites a brief prayer and says: Redeem, Lord, Your people, the remnant of Israel, at every transition [parashat ha’ibur], the meaning of which will be discussed in the Gemara. May their needs be before You. Blessed are You, Lord, Who listens to prayer.

mishnayos.summary: When we daven, we face toward the Beis HaMikdash. Someone riding a donkey should get off; if he can't, he turns his face, and if he can't do that, he thinks about the Kodesh HaKodashim.

chunks.en: If he was riding on a donkey,
he should get off to daven.
And if he cannot get off,
he should turn his face toward Yerushalayim,

chunks.he: וְאִם אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לְהַחֲזִיר אֶת פָּנָיו,
chunks.en: and if he cannot turn his face,
he should point his heart
toward the Kodesh HaKodashim.

words.note: The Kodesh HaKodashim, the holiest room in the Beis HaMikdash.

mishnayos.english: While praying, one must face toward the direction of the Holy Temple. One who was riding on a donkey should dismount and pray calmly. If he is unable to dismount, he should turn his face toward the direction of the Temple. If he is unable to turn his face, it is sufficient that he focus his heart opposite the Holy of Holies.

mishnayos.summary: Someone traveling on a boat, wagon, or raft who can't turn to face Yerushalayim should think about the Kodesh HaKodashim while he davens.

chunks.en: If he was sitting in a boat
or in a wagon or on a raft,
he should point his heart
toward the Kodesh HaKodashim.

words.note: The Kodesh HaKodashim, the holiest room in the Beis HaMikdash.

mishnayos.english: Similarly, one who was traveling in a ship or on a wagon or on a raft [asda] and is unable to turn and face in the direction of Jerusalem, should focus his heart opposite the Holy of Holies.

mishnayos.summary: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah says Musaf is said only with a community minyan. The Chachamim say it is said with or without one.

chunks.en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah says,

words.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah was a great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.he: אֵין תְּפִלַּת הַמּוּסָפִין אֶלָּא בְּחֶבֶר עִיר.
chunks.en: Musaf is said only with the town's group.

words.note: The extra tefillah on Shabbos, Yom Tov, and Rosh Chodesh.
The town's minyan that davens together.

chunks.en: And the Sages say,
with the town's group or without the town's group.
Rabbi Yehuda says in his name,

words.note: Rabbi Yehuda was a great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: any place where there is a town group,
a person davening alone does not have to say Musaf.

mishnayos.english: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says: The additional prayer is only recited in a city where there is a quorum of ten [ḥever ir]. The Rabbis say: One may recite the additional prayer with a ḥever ir or without a ḥever ir. Rabbi Yehuda says another opinion in his name, the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya: Any place where there is a ḥever ir, an individual is completely exempt from reciting the additional prayer.

mishnayos.summary: How to get ready for davening: think seriously first, and once you start, don't stop for anything.

chunks.en: We only stand up to daven
with a serious, humble feeling.
The very pious people of long ago would wait

words.note: Very holy people who did more than they had to.

chunks.en: one hour and then daven,
so they could turn their hearts to Hashem.

words.note: "HaMakom" is a name for Hashem, Who is everywhere.

chunks.en: Even if the king says hello to him,
he should not answer him.
And even if a snake is wrapped around his heel,
he should not stop.

mishnayos.english: One may only stand and begin to pray from an approach of gravity and submission. There is a tradition that the early generations of pious men would wait one hour, in order to reach the solemn frame of mind appropriate for prayer, and then pray, so that they would focus their hearts toward their Father in Heaven. Standing in prayer is standing before God and, as such, even if the king greets him, he should not respond to him; and even if a snake is wrapped on his heel, he should not interrupt his prayer.

mishnayos.summary: Where in Shemoneh Esrei we add words about rain and the Havdalah prayer on Motzei Shabbos.

chunks.en: We mention Hashem's power of rain in the bracha about bringing the dead back to life,

words.note: The second bracha of Shemoneh Esrei, "Mechayei Hameisim."

chunks.en: and we ask for rain in the bracha for a good year,

words.note: The bracha "Bareich Aleinu," asking for good crops.

chunks.en: and Havdalah goes in the bracha "Atah Chonen," about wisdom.

words.note: Words that separate Shabbos or Yom Tov from the weekday.
The bracha "Atah Chonen," asking for wisdom.

chunks.en: Rabbi Akiva says,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: we say it as a fourth bracha all by itself.
Rabbi Eliezer says, it goes in "Modim," the thank-you bracha.

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.
The bracha "Modim," where we thank Hashem.

mishnayos.english: This mishna speaks of additions to the standard formula of the Amida prayer and the blessings in which they are incorporated. One mentions the might of the rains and recites: He makes the wind blow and the rain fall, in the second blessing of the Amida prayer, the blessing of the revival of the dead. And the request for rain: And grant dew and rain as a blessing, in the ninth blessing of the Amida prayer, the blessing of the years. And the prayer of distinction [havdala], between the holy and the profane recited in the evening prayer following Shabbat and festivals, in the fourth blessing of the Amida prayer: Who graciously grants knowledge. Rabbi Akiva says: Havdala is recited as an independent fourth blessing. Rabbi Eliezer says that it is recited in the seventeenth blessing of the Amida prayer, the blessing of thanksgiving.

mishnayos.summary: Some wrong things a chazzan might say, and what to do if the chazzan makes a mistake.

chunks.he: הָאוֹמֵר עַל קַן צִפּוֹר יַגִּיעוּ רַחֲמֶיךָ,
chunks.en: Someone who says, "Your mercy reaches even a bird's nest,"

words.note: The mitzvah to send away a mother bird before taking the eggs.

chunks.en: or "Your Name should be mentioned for the good,"
or "Modim, Modim" twice,
we make him be quiet.
If the chazzan leading the davening makes a mistake,

words.note: The aron where the Sefer Torah is; the chazzan stands in front of it.

chunks.en: someone else should take his place,
and he should not say "no thanks" at that time.
Where does he start?
From the beginning of the bracha where the mistake was.

mishnayos.english: Concluding the laws of prayer in this tractate, the mishna raises several prayer-related matters. This mishna speaks of certain innovations in the prayer formula that warrant the silencing of a communal prayer leader who attempts to introduce them in his prayers, as their content tends toward heresy. One who recites in his supplication: Just as Your mercy is extended to a bird’s nest, as You have commanded us to send away the mother before taking her chicks or eggs (Deuteronomy 22:6–7), so too extend Your mercy to us; and one who recites: May Your name be mentioned with the good or one who recites: We give thanks, we give thanks twice, they silence him. This mishna and the next one deal with the communal prayer leader. (If one says: “May the good bless You,” this is a path of heresy.) One who is passing before the ark, as prayer leader, and erred, another should immediately pass in his place, and at that moment, this replacement should not refuse in the interest of courtesy. The Amida prayer was interrupted and he should replace him as quickly as possible. From where does the replacement commence? From the beginning of the blessing in which the former had erred.

mishnayos.summary: The chazzan should be careful not to get mixed up, so he doesn't answer Amen to the Kohanim or do Birkas Kohanim himself.

chunks.en: The chazzan leading the davening

words.note: The aron where the Sefer Torah is; the chazzan stands in front of it.

chunks.en: should not answer Amen after the Kohanim's bracha,

words.note: Kohanim bless the people with Birkas Kohanim.

chunks.en: because he might get mixed up.

chunks.he: וְאִם אֵין שָׁם כֹּהֵן אֶלָּא הוּא,
chunks.en: And if he is the only Kohen there,
he should not raise his hands to bless.
But if he is sure
that he can raise his hands to bless
and go back to his davening, he may do it.

mishnayos.english: In order to prevent the prayer leader from erring in his prayer, it was said that one who passes before the ark should not respond amen after the blessing of the priests, because of potential confusion. Since the mishna is describing a situation in which he was praying without a prayer book, responding amen would interrupt the order of the prayer and potentially lead him to begin a different blessing. For this reason, even if there is no priest other than the communal prayer leader, he does not lift his hands to bless the people, lest he become confused. And, however, if he is certain that he can lift his hands and resume his prayer without becoming confused, he is permitted to recite the blessing.

mishnayos.summary: A mistake in davening is a bad sign. Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa could tell if his prayers for sick people were accepted.

chunks.en: If someone davens and makes a mistake,
it is a bad sign for him.
And if he is the chazzan,

words.note: The chazzan, who davens for everyone.

chunks.en: it is a bad sign for the people who sent him,
because a person's messenger is like the person himself.
They said about
Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah, famous for his holy prayers.

chunks.en: that when he davened for sick people, he would say,
"This one will live, and this one will die."
They asked him,
"How do you know?"
He told them,
"If my prayer flows smoothly from my mouth,
I know that it was accepted.
And if not,
I know that it was not accepted."

mishnayos.english: Concluding its discussion of the halakhot of prayer, the mishna discusses less practical aspects of prayer. One who prays and realizes that he erred in his prayer, it is a bad omen for him; it indicates to him that his prayer was not accepted. And if he who erred is the communal prayer leader, it is a bad omen for those who sent him, because a person’s agent has legal status equivalent to his own. On a similar note, they said about Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa that he would pray on behalf of the sick and immediately after his prayer he would say: This one shall recover from his illness and live and this one shall die. When they said to him: From where do you know? He said to them: If my prayer is fluent in my mouth as I recite it and there are no errors, I know that my prayer is accepted. And if not, I know that my prayer is rejected.

mishnayos.summary: Which bracha we make before eating fruit, wine, bread, and vegetables.

chunks.en: How do we make a bracha on fruits?
On fruit from a tree, one says,
"Borei pri ha'etz" (Who creates fruit of the tree),
except for wine,

chunks.he: שֶׁעַל הַיַּיִן אוֹמֵר בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הַגָּפֶן.
chunks.en: because on wine one says "Borei pri hagafen" (Who creates fruit of the vine).
And on food that grows from the ground, one says
"Borei pri ha'adamah" (Who creates fruit of the ground),
except for bread,
because on bread one says
"Hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz" (Who brings bread out of the earth).

chunks.he: וְעַל הַיְרָקוֹת אוֹמֵר בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה.
chunks.en: And on vegetables one says "Borei pri ha'adamah."
Rabbi Yehudah says,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: "Who creates all kinds of herbs."

mishnayos.english: This mishna discusses the blessings recited over various foods. How does one recite a blessing over fruits? Over different fruits that grow on a tree one recites: Who creates fruit of the tree, with the exception of wine. Although wine is produced from fruit of the tree, due to its significance, its blessing differs from other fruits of the tree. Over wine one recites: Who creates fruit of the vine. Over fruits that grow from the earth, one recites: Who creates fruit of the ground, with the exception of bread. Bread, too, is significant and its blessing differs from other fruits of the ground, as over bread one recites: Who brings forth bread from the earth. Over herbs and leafy vegetables one recites: Who creates fruit of the ground. Rabbi Yehuda says that there is room to distinguish between fruits that grow from the earth, herbs, and leafy vegetables. Although they are all fruit of the ground, since they have different qualities, the blessing on the latter is: Who creates various kinds of herbs.

mishnayos.summary: If you made the wrong bracha on food, sometimes it still counts, and "Shehakol" works for everything.

chunks.en: If someone said on tree fruit
"Borei pri ha'adamah," it still counts.

words.note: He did the mitzvah and does not need to say it again.

chunks.he: וְעַל פֵּרוֹת הָאָרֶץ בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָעֵץ,
chunks.en: But if he said on food from the ground "Borei pri ha'etz,"
it does not count.

chunks.he: עַל כֻּלָּם אִם אָמַר שֶׁהַכֹּל נִהְיָה, יָצָא:
chunks.en: On any food, if he said "Shehakol nihyah bidvaro," it counts.

words.note: The bracha "Shehakol," meaning everything came to be by Hashem's word.

mishnayos.english: This mishna discusses how, after the fact, a more general blessing exempts one from the obligation to recite a more specific one. One who recited: Who creates fruit of the ground, over fruit of the tree, fulfilled his obligation. One who recited: Who creates fruit of the tree, over fruits of the earth, did not fulfill his obligation. And over all food items, one who recited: By whose word all things came to be, fulfilled his obligation.

mishnayos.summary: Foods that don't grow from the ground get the bracha "Shehakol."

chunks.he: עַל דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין גִּדּוּלוֹ מִן הָאָרֶץ
chunks.en: On something that does not grow from the ground
one says "Shehakol."
On vinegar, and on fruit that fell off the tree too early,

words.note: Dates that dried up and fell before they got ripe.

chunks.en: and on locusts, one says "Shehakol."

words.note: A kind of grasshopper; some kinds are kosher.

chunks.en: On milk and on cheese
and on eggs, one says "Shehakol."
Rabbi Yehudah says,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: anything that comes from a kind of curse, like spoiled food,
we do not make a bracha on it.

mishnayos.english: And over a food item whose growth is not from the ground, one recites: By whose word all things came to be. And over vinegar, wine that fermented and spoiled, and over novelot, dates that spoiled, and over locusts, one recites: By whose word all things came to be. So too, over milk, and over cheese, and over eggs, one recites: By whose word all things came to be. Rabbi Yehuda says: Over any food item that is a type resulting from a curse, one does not recite a blessing over it at all. None of the items listed exist under normal conditions, and they come about as the result of a curse.

mishnayos.summary: If you have many foods in front of you, which one do you make the bracha on first?

chunks.en: If there were many kinds of food in front of him,
Rabbi Yehudah says,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: if one of them is from the seven special foods of Eretz Yisrael,

words.note: The seven special foods of Eretz Yisrael, like grapes, figs, and dates.

chunks.en: he makes the bracha on that one.
And the Sages say,
he makes the bracha on whichever one he wants.

mishnayos.english: On a different note: If there were many types of food before him, over which food should he recite a blessing first? Rabbi Yehuda says: If there is one of the seven species for which Eretz Yisrael was praised among them, he recites the first blessing over it. And the Rabbis say: He recites a blessing over whichever of them he wants.

mishnayos.summary: When one bracha covers other foods too, so you don't need a new bracha.

chunks.en: If he made a bracha on the wine before the meal,
it also covers the wine after the meal.

words.note: He doesn't need another bracha for it.

chunks.en: If he made a bracha on the snacks before the meal,

words.note: Small foods eaten before or after a meal, like appetizers.

chunks.en: it also covers the snacks after the meal.
If he made a bracha on the bread,
it covers the snacks.
But a bracha on the snacks
does not cover the bread.
Beis Shammai say,

words.note: Beis Shammai are the students of Shammai, a great early Rabbi.

chunks.en: it does not even cover a cooked dish.

mishnayos.english: This mishna explains those cases and those circumstances in which blessings recited over particular foods exempt other foods at the meal from the requirement to recite a blessing over them. One who recited a blessing over the wine that one drank before the meal, with that blessing he exempted the wine that he drinks after the meal. Similarly, one who recited a blessing over the appetizers that one ate before the meal, with that blessing he exempted the appetizers that he eats after the meal. One who recited a blessing over the bread exempted the appetizers, as they are considered secondary to the bread. However, one who recited a blessing over the appetizers did not exempt the bread. Beit Shammai say: The blessing recited over the appetizers did not exempt even a cooked dish that he eats during the meal.

mishnayos.summary: When people eat together, sometimes one person makes the bracha for everyone.

chunks.en: If people were sitting to eat,
each one makes his own bracha.
If they leaned on couches together for a meal, one makes the bracha for all of them.

words.note: Long ago, people ate a real meal together leaning on couches.

chunks.en: If wine was brought to them during the meal,
each one makes his own bracha.
If it came after the meal,
one makes the bracha for all of them.
And that same person says the bracha on the nice-smelling spices,

words.note: Sweet-smelling spices burned on coals after a meal.

chunks.en: even though they only bring
the spices after the meal is over.

mishnayos.english: An additional halakha is cited: If several people were sitting to eat not in the framework of a joint meal, each recites a blessing for himself. If they were reclined on divans to eat, which renders it a joint meal, one recites a blessing on behalf of them all. Additionally: If wine came before them during the meal, each and every diner recites a blessing over the wine for himself. If the wine came after the meal, one recites a blessing on behalf of them all. And he, who recited the blessing over the wine, also says the blessing over the incense [mugmar], although they only bring the incense to the diners after the meal.

mishnayos.summary: When one food is the main food and another is just a side, we make the bracha on the main food.

chunks.he: הֵבִיאוּ לְפָנָיו מָלִיחַ בַּתְּחִלָּה וּפַת עִמּוֹ,
chunks.en: If they brought him salty fish first, with bread alongside it,

words.note: Salty fish, eaten with bread to soften the taste.

chunks.he: מְבָרֵךְ עַל הַמָּלִיחַ וּפוֹטֵר אֶת הַפַּת,
chunks.en: he makes the bracha on the salty fish, and that covers the bread,
because the bread is just a side to it.
This is the rule:
whenever there is a main food with a side food,

chunks.he: מְבָרֵךְ עַל הָעִקָּר וּפוֹטֵר אֶת הַטְּפֵלָה:
chunks.en: you make the bracha on the main food, and that covers the side food.

mishnayos.english: If they brought salted food before him to eat first and bread with it, he recites a blessing over the salted food and thereby exempts the bread, because the salted food is primary while the bread is secondary to it. This is the principle: Any food that is primary and a secondary food is with it, one recites a blessing over the primary and, in so doing, exempts the secondary from its own blessing.

mishnayos.summary: Which bracha to say after eating special fruits, vegetables, or drinking water.

chunks.en: If someone ate figs, grapes, and pomegranates,
he says after them the three brachos, like full bentching,

words.note: The three main brachos of bentching after a bread meal.

chunks.en: so says Rabban Gamliel.

words.note: "Rabban" is a title for the head of the Sages.
A great Rabbi of the Mishnah, the leader of the Sages.

chunks.en: And the Sages say,
one bracha that is a short form of the three.

words.note: This is "Al Hamichya / Al Ha'etz," a short after-bracha.

chunks.en: Rabbi Akiva says,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: even if he ate cooked vegetables and that is his meal,
he says after it the three brachos.
Someone who drinks water because he is thirsty
says "Shehakol nihyeh bidvaro" (everything came to be by His word).
Rabbi Tarfon says,

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: "Borei nefashos rabos" (Who creates many living things).

mishnayos.english: One who ate from the fruit for which Eretz Yisrael was praised, grapes and figs and pomegranates, recites the three blessings of Grace after Meals, as he would after eating bread; this is the statement of Rabban Gamliel. And the Rabbis say: One need only recite one blessing abridged from the three blessings of Grace after Meals. Rabbi Akiva says: The three blessings of Grace after Meals are not restricted to bread; rather, even if one ate boiled vegetables, but it is his primary sustenance, he recites the three blessings of Grace after Meals. Additionally: One who drinks water to quench his thirst recites: By whose word all things came to be. Rabbi Tarfon says: He recites: Who creates the many forms of life and their needs.

mishnayos.summary: When three people eat a meal together, they must make a zimmun before bentching. The mishnah lists who counts toward the three and who does not.

chunks.en: Three people who ate together
must make a zimmun.

words.note: Inviting the others to bentch together, saying "Let us bless."

chunks.en: If one ate demai,

words.note: Food bought from someone who might not have taken off maaser.

chunks.en: or first maaser that had its terumah taken off,

words.note: A tenth of the crops given to the Levi'im.
The part of the crops given to the Kohanim.

chunks.en: or second maaser or holy things that were redeemed,

words.note: A tenth of the crops eaten in Yerushalayim.
Things given to the Beis HaMikdash.

chunks.en: or the waiter who ate a kezayis,

words.note: A small amount of food, about the size of an olive.

chunks.en: or a Kuti — they count for the zimmun.

words.note: A Samaritan, a group who kept some of the Torah's mitzvos.

chunks.en: But if one ate tevel,

words.note: Food that terumah and maaser were not yet taken from.

chunks.en: or first maaser that did not have its terumah taken off,
or second maaser or holy things that were not redeemed,
or the waiter who ate less than a kezayis,
or a non-Jew — they do not count for the zimmun.

mishnayos.english: This mishna sets out the essential halakhot pertaining to the invitation to recite Grace after Meals after a joint meal [zimmun]: Three people who ate as one are required to form a zimmun and recite Grace after Meals. If, among the diners, one ate doubtfully tithed produce [demai], and first tithe from which its teruma was already taken, or second tithe, and consecrated food that were redeemed and therefore permitted to be eaten; and even the waiter who served the meal to the diners and who ate at least an olive-bulk from the meal, and the Samaritan [Kuti] who ate with two others at a meal; each of these people is included among the three to obligate those with whom they ate in a zimmun. However, one who ate untithed produce [tevel], and first tithe from which its teruma was not separated, and second tithe, and consecrated food that were not redeemed, and the waiter who did not eat an olive-bulk, and the gentile who ate with two Jews, none of these people is included among the three to obligate those with whom they ate in a zimmun.

mishnayos.summary: Women, slaves, and children do not count toward a men's zimmun. The mishnah also says how much a person must eat to count.

chunks.en: Women, slaves, and children —
we do not count them for the zimmun.
How much must one eat to count for the zimmun?
Even a kezayis.

words.note: A small amount of food, about the size of an olive.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehudah says:

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: It must be as much as an egg.

mishnayos.english: Women, slaves, and minors do not obligate those with whom they ate in a zimmun. How much must one eat to obligate those with whom he ate in a zimmun? An olive-bulk of food suffices to obligate those with whom they ate in a zimmun. Rabbi Yehuda says: An egg-bulk is the minimum measure to obligate those with whom they ate in a zimmun.

mishnayos.summary: The words of the zimmun change depending on how many people ate together. The more people, the more names of Hashem are added.

chunks.en: How do we make the zimmun?
With three, the leader says "Let us bless."
With three plus himself,
he says "Bless!"
With ten, he says "Let us bless our God."
With ten plus himself,
he says "Bless!"
It is the same for ten or for a hundred thousand.
With a hundred, he says
"Let us bless Hashem our God."
With a hundred plus himself,
he says "Bless!"

chunks.he: בְּאֶלֶף, אוֹמֵר נְבָרֵךְ לַייָ אֱלֹהֵינוּ אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל.
chunks.en: With a thousand, he says "Let us bless Hashem our God, the God of Israel."
With a thousand plus himself,
he says "Bless!"
With ten thousand, he says
"Let us bless Hashem our God, the God of Israel,
the God of the heavenly armies, Who sits above the Keruvim,

words.note: The golden angel figures on top of the Aron in the Beis HaMikdash.

chunks.en: for the food that we ate."
With ten thousand plus himself,
he says "Bless!"
Just like the way he says the bracha,
so the others answer after him:
"Blessed is Hashem our God, the God of Israel,
the God of the heavenly armies, Who sits above the Keruvim,
for the food that we ate."
Rabbi Yosi HaGelili says:

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: The words depend on how big the crowd is,
as the pasuk says: "In crowds, bless God,
Hashem, from the source of Israel." (Tehillim 68)
Rabbi Akiva said:

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: Look at what we do in shul:
whether there are many people or few, the chazzan says
"Bless Hashem."
Rabbi Yishmael says:

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: "Bless Hashem, the Blessed One."

mishnayos.english: The mishna delineates distinctions in the halakhot of the zimmun blessing, based on the number of people present. How does one recite the zimmun? In a group of three people, the one reciting the zimmun says: Let us bless the One from Whose food we have eaten. In a group of three people and him, the one reciting the zimmun says: Bless the One from Whose food we have eaten, as even without him there are enough people to recite the zimmun. With the increase in the number of participants, the blessing is more complex. In a group of ten people, the one reciting the zimmun says: Let us bless our God. In a group of ten people and him, the one reciting the zimmun says: Bless our God. This formula is recited both in a group of ten and in a group of one hundred thousand. In a group of one hundred people, the one reciting the zimmun says: Let us bless the Lord our God. In a group of one hundred people and him, the one reciting the zimmun says: Bless the Lord our God. In a group of one thousand people, the one reciting the zimmun says: Let us bless the Lord our God, the God of Israel. In a group of one thousand people and him, he says: Bless the Lord our God, the God of Israel. In a group of ten thousand people, the one reciting the zimmun says: Let us bless the Lord our God, the God of Israel, the God of Hosts, Who sits upon the cherubs, for the food that we have eaten. In a group of ten thousand people and him, the one reciting the zimmun says: Bless the Lord our God, the God of Israel, the God of Hosts, Who sits upon the cherubs, for the food that we have eaten. The principle is that just as he recites the blessing, so too those present recite in response: Blessed be the Lord our God, the God of Israel, the God of Hosts, Who sits upon the cherubs, for the food that we have eaten. On a similar note, Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says: According to the size of the crowd, they recite the blessing, as it is stated: “Bless you God in full assemblies, even the Lord, you who are from the fountain of Israel” (Psalms 68:27). Rabbi Akiva said that there are no distinctions based on the size of the crowd: What do we find in the synagogue? Both when there are many and when there are few, as long as there is a quorum of ten, the prayer leader says: Bless [barekhu] the Lord. Rabbi Yishmael said that in the synagogue, one recites: Bless the Lord the blessed One.

mishnayos.summary: A group that ate together may only split up into smaller groups for zimmun if each smaller group can still say the same zimmun.

chunks.en: Three people who ate together
are not allowed to split up,
and the same for four,
and the same for five.
Six may split up,
until there are ten.
And ten may not split up
until there are twenty.

mishnayos.english: Three people who ate as one are not permitted to divide and recite Grace after Meals individually; rather, they recite the zimmun together. And the same is true of four who ate together, and the same is true of five. However, a group of six, up to but not including ten people who ate as one, may divide into two groups, each reciting its own zimmun. And a group of ten may not divide into two groups until there are twenty people present. The general principle is that a group may not divide unless the smaller groups will be able to recite the same zimmun formula that the whole group would have recited.

mishnayos.summary: Two groups eating in one house can join for zimmun if they can see each other. Also, Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages argue about making a bracha on wine with no water added.

chunks.he: שְׁתֵּי חֲבוּרוֹת שֶׁהָיוּ אוֹכְלוֹת בְּבַיִת אֶחָד,
chunks.en: Two groups that were eating in one house,

chunks.he: בִּזְמַן שֶׁמִּקְצָתָן רוֹאִין אֵלּוּ אֶת אֵלּוּ,
chunks.en: when some of them can see each other,
they join together for a zimmun.

words.note: Inviting the others to bentch together, saying "Let us bless."

chunks.en: But if not,
these make a zimmun for themselves,
and those make a zimmun for themselves.
We do not make the bracha on wine
until water is put into it,
says Rabbi Eliezer.

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: But the Sages say: we do make the bracha.

mishnayos.english: The mishna states a halakha with regard to two groups joining together: Two groups that were eating in one house, when some members of each group can see each other, they may combine to form a zimmun. And if not, these recite a zimmun for themselves and those recite a zimmun for themselves. The mishna also speaks of the blessing over wine: One does not recite a blessing over wine until he adds water to it, that is the statement of Rabbi Eliezer. Undiluted wine is too strong to drink and a blessing is inappropriate. And the Rabbis say: Since it is possible to drink undiluted wine, one recites a blessing over it.

mishnayos.summary: This perek lists arguments between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel about meals. The first is about Kiddush: which bracha comes first, the one on the day or the one on the wine.

chunks.en: These are the things
that Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel argue about

words.note: The students of Shammai, a great Rabbi long ago.
The students of Hillel, a great Rabbi long ago; we usually follow them.

chunks.en: at a meal.
Beis Shammai say:
first he makes the bracha on the day (Shabbos or Yom Tov),
and after that he makes the bracha on the wine.
And Beis Hillel say:
first he makes the bracha on the wine,
and after that he makes the bracha on the day.

mishnayos.english: These are the matters of dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel with regard to the halakhot of a meal: One dispute concerns the order of blessings in kiddush. Beit Shammai say: When one recites kiddush over wine, one recites a blessing over the sanctification of the day and recites a blessing over the wine thereafter. And Beit Hillel say: One recites a blessing over the wine and recites a blessing over the day thereafter.

mishnayos.summary: Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel argue about what comes first before a meal: washing hands or pouring the cup of wine.

chunks.en: Beis Shammai say:

words.note: The students of Shammai, a great Rabbi long ago.

chunks.en: first we wash our hands,
and after that we pour the cup of wine.
And Beis Hillel say:

words.note: The students of Hillel, a great Rabbi long ago; we usually follow them.

chunks.en: first we pour the cup of wine,
and after that we wash our hands.

mishnayos.english: Similarly, Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai disagree with regard to drinking wine before a meal. Beit Shammai say: One washes his hands and mixes water with the wine in the cup thereafter, and Beit Hillel say: One mixes water with the wine in the cup and only washes his hands thereafter. The basis of this particular dispute is with regard to the laws of ritual purity, as the Gemara will explain below.

mishnayos.summary: After washing hands, where should a person put the towel? Beis Shammai say on the table, and Beis Hillel say on the cushion.

chunks.en: Beis Shammai say:

words.note: The students of Shammai, a great Rabbi long ago.

chunks.he: מְקַנֵּחַ יָדָיו בַּמַּפָּה וּמַנִּיחָהּ עַל הַשֻּׁלְחָן.
chunks.en: he dries his hands with a towel and puts it on the table.
And Beis Hillel say:

words.note: The students of Hillel, a great Rabbi long ago; we usually follow them.

chunks.en: he puts it on the cushion.

mishnayos.english: Also with regard to the laws of ritual purity, Beit Shammai say: After washing, one dries his hands with a cloth and places it on the table. And Beit Hillel say: One places it on the cushion upon which he is sitting.

mishnayos.summary: After the meal, what comes first: sweeping the floor or washing hands before bentching?

chunks.en: Beis Shammai say:

words.note: The students of Shammai, a great Rabbi long ago.

chunks.en: first we sweep the house,
and after that we wash our hands.
And Beis Hillel say:

words.note: The students of Hillel, a great Rabbi long ago; we usually follow them.

chunks.en: first we wash our hands,
and after that we sweep the house.

mishnayos.english: Similarly, Beit Shammai say: One sweeps the area of the house where the meal took place and he washes his hands with the final waters before Grace after Meals thereafter. And Beit Hillel say: One washes his hands and sweeps the house thereafter.

mishnayos.summary: If a meal goes on until Shabbos is over, there are four brachos to say. Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel argue about their order, and about the words of the bracha on the fire.

chunks.en: Beis Shammai say the order is:

words.note: The students of Shammai, a great Rabbi long ago.

chunks.en: candle, bentching, spices, and Havdalah.

words.note: The bracha after the meal, Birkas HaMazon.
The bracha that separates Shabbos from the weekdays.

chunks.en: And Beis Hillel say:

words.note: The students of Hillel, a great Rabbi long ago; we usually follow them.

chunks.en: candle, spices, bentching, and Havdalah.
Beis Shammai say the bracha on the fire is:
"Who created the light of the fire."
And Beis Hillel say:
"Who creates the lights of the fire."

mishnayos.english: Just as they dispute the order of the blessings in kiddush, they dispute the order of the blessings in havdala. If a meal continued until the conclusion of Shabbat, Beit Shammai say: One recites the blessing over the candle, then the Grace after Meals blessing, then the blessing over the spices, and finally the blessing of havdala. And Beit Hillel say: The order is candle, spices, Grace after Meals, and havdala. With regard to the blessing over the candle, Beit Shammai say: Who created [bara] the light of fire. And Beit Hillel say: Who creates [boreh] the lights of fire.

mishnayos.summary: Some candles and spices may not be used for the Havdalah brachos, like those used for idols. Also, we only make the bracha on a candle when we can use its light.

chunks.en: We do not make a bracha on the candle

chunks.he: וְלֹא עַל הַבְּשָׂמִים שֶׁל עוֹבְדֵי כוֹכָבִים,
chunks.en: or on the spices of idol worshippers,

words.note: People who worshipped stars and idols.

chunks.en: nor on the candle
or the spices used for the dead,

words.note: Candles and spices used to honor a person who passed away.

chunks.en: nor on the candle
or the spices
that are in front of an idol.

words.note: Avodah zarah means idol worship.

chunks.en: We do not make the bracha on the candle
until we can enjoy its light.

mishnayos.english: One may neither recite a blessing over the candle nor over the spices of gentiles, nor over the candle nor the spices designated to pay respects to the dead, nor over the candle nor the spices of idolatry. The mishna cites another halakha with regard to the blessing over the candle: And one does not recite the blessing over the candle until he derives benefit from its light.

mishnayos.summary: If someone ate and forgot to bentch and left, where should he bentch? Also, there is a time limit for bentching.

chunks.en: Someone who ate and forgot and did not bentch:
Beis Shammai say:

words.note: The students of Shammai, a great Rabbi long ago.

chunks.en: he must go back to his place and bentch.
And Beis Hillel say:

words.note: The students of Hillel, a great Rabbi long ago; we usually follow them.

chunks.en: he should bentch in the place where he remembered.
Until when can he bentch?
Until the food is digested
in his stomach.

mishnayos.english: The mishna cites an additional dispute: One who ate and forgot and did not recite a blessing; Beit Shammai say: He returns to the place where he ate and recites the blessing. Beit Hillel say: That is unnecessary. He recites the blessing at the place where he remembered. Both agree, however, that there is a limit with regard to how long after eating one may recite Grace after Meals. And until when does he recite the blessing? Until the food is digested in his intestines.

mishnayos.summary: If wine is brought after the meal and there is only one cup, which bracha comes first? Also, when do we answer Amen to someone's bracha?

chunks.en: If wine came to them after the meal
and there is only that one cup,
Beis Shammai say:

words.note: The students of Shammai, a great Rabbi long ago.

chunks.en: first he makes the bracha on the wine,
and after that he bentches on the food.
And Beis Hillel say:

words.note: The students of Hillel, a great Rabbi long ago; we usually follow them.

chunks.en: first he bentches on the food,
and after that he makes the bracha on the wine.
We answer Amen after a Jew who makes a bracha,
