chunks.he: וְאֵין עוֹנִין אָמֵן אַחַר הַכּוּתִי הַמְבָרֵךְ,
chunks.en: but we do not answer Amen after a Kuti who makes a bracha

words.note: A Samaritan, a group who kept some of the Torah's mitzvos.

chunks.en: until we hear the whole bracha.

mishnayos.english: Wine came before the diners after the meal; if only that cup of wine is there, Beit Shammai say: One recites a blessing over the wine and recites a blessing over the food, Grace after Meals, thereafter. And Beit Hillel say: One recites a blessing over the food and recites a blessing over the wine thereafter. And one answers amen after a Jew who recites a blessing even if he did not hear the entire blessing, and one does not answer amen after a Samaritan [Kuti] who recites a blessing until he hears the whole blessing in its entirety, as perhaps the Kuti introduced an element inconsistent with the Jewish faith in that section of the blessing that he did not hear.

mishnayos.summary: When you see a place where Hashem did a miracle for the Jewish people, or a place where idol worship was wiped out, you say a special bracha.

chunks.he: הָרוֹאֶה מָקוֹם שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוּ בוֹ נִסִּים לְיִשְׂרָאֵל,
chunks.en: Someone who sees a place where miracles happened for the Jewish people
says: Blessed is the One who did miracles
for our fathers in this place.
A place where idol worship was pulled out,

words.note: Avodah zarah means worshipping idols instead of Hashem.

chunks.he: אוֹמֵר בָּרוּךְ שֶׁעָקַר עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה מֵאַרְצֵנוּ:
chunks.en: you say: Blessed is the One who pulled idol worship out of our land.

mishnayos.english: This mishna, which includes all of this chapter’s mishnayot, contains a series of blessings and halakhot that are not recited at specific times, but rather in response to various experiences and events.MISHNA: One who sees a place where miracles occurred on Israel’s behalf recites: Blessed…Who performed miracles for our forefathers in this place. One who sees a place from which idolatry was eradicated recites: Blessed…Who eradicated idolatry from our land.

mishnayos.summary: There are brachos for amazing things in nature, like thunder, lightning, mountains and seas, and for good news and bad news.

chunks.en: On comets,

words.note: Zikin are shooting stars or comets streaking across the sky.

chunks.en: and on earthquakes,
and on lightning,
and on thunder,
and on strong winds,

chunks.he: אוֹמֵר בָּרוּךְ שֶׁכֹּחוֹ וּגְבוּרָתוֹ מָלֵא עוֹלָם.
chunks.en: you say: Blessed is the One whose strength and power fill the world.
On mountains,
and on hills,
and on seas,
and on rivers,
and on deserts,
you say: Blessed is the One who made the world at the beginning.
Rabbi Yehudah says:

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: Someone who sees the Great Sea says:

words.note: The Great Sea is the Mediterranean Sea, west of Eretz Yisrael.

chunks.en: Blessed is the One who made the Great Sea,
but only when he sees it once in a while.
On rain and on good news
you say: Blessed is the One who is good and does good,
and on bad news you say:
Blessed is the true Judge.

mishnayos.english: One who sees conspicuous natural occurrences recites a blessing. For zikin and zeva’ot, which the Gemara will discuss below, for lightning, thunder, and gale force winds, manifestations of the power of the Creator, one recites: Blessed…Whose strength and power fill the world. For extraordinary (Rambam) mountains, hills, seas, rivers, and deserts, one recites: Blessed…Author of creation. Consistent with his opinion that a separate blessing should be instituted for each individual species, Rabbi Yehuda says: One who sees the great sea recites a special blessing: Blessed…Who made the great sea. As with all blessings of this type, one only recites it when he sees the sea intermittently, not on a regular basis. For rain and other good tidings, one recites the special blessing: Blessed…Who is good and Who does good. Even for bad tidings, one recites a special blessing: Blessed…the true Judge.

mishnayos.summary: When you get a new house or new things you say Shehecheyanu. Davening for something that already happened is a wasted tefillah.

chunks.en: If someone built a new house,
or bought new things,
he says: Blessed... Shehecheyanu, who kept us alive.

words.note: Shehecheyanu is the bracha we say on something new or a special time.

chunks.en: He says a bracha on a bad thing even if it may turn out good,
and on a good thing even if it may turn out bad.
Someone who cries out about what already happened,
that is a wasted tefillah.
How so?
If his wife was expecting a baby,

chunks.he: וְאָמַר, יְהִי רָצוֹן שֶׁתֵּלֵד אִשְׁתִּי זָכָר,
chunks.en: and he said: May it be Hashem's will that my wife has a boy,
that is a wasted tefillah.
If he was coming on the road and he heard
the sound of screaming in the city,
and he said: May it be Hashem's will
that these are not my family,
that is a wasted tefillah.

mishnayos.english: Similarly, when one built a new house or purchased new vessels, he recites: Blessed…Who has given us life, sustained us, and brought us to this time. The mishna articulates a general principle: One recites a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he does for the good. In other words, one recites the appropriate blessing for the trouble that he is experiencing at present despite the fact that it may conceal some positive element in the future. Similarly, one must recite a blessing for the good that befalls him just as for the bad. The mishna states: And one who cries out over the past in an attempt to change that which has already occurred, it is a vain prayer. For example, one whose wife was pregnant and he says: May it be God’s will that my wife will give birth to a male child, it is a vain prayer. Or one who was walking on the path home and he heard the sound of a scream in the city, and he says: May it be God’s will that this scream will not be from my house, it is a vain prayer. In both cases, the event already occurred.

mishnayos.summary: When you go into a big city, you daven when you go in and when you come out.

chunks.en: Someone who goes into a big city says two tefillos,

words.note: A kerach is a large walled city, which could be a dangerous place.

chunks.en: one when he goes in and one when he goes out.
Ben Azzai says:

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: Four: two when he goes in and two when he goes out.
He says thank you for what already happened,
and he cries out to Hashem for what is still coming.

mishnayos.english: The Sages also said: One who enters a large city, the Gemara explains below that this is in a case where entering the city is dangerous, recites two prayers: One upon his entrance, that he may enter in peace, and one upon his exit, that he may leave in peace. Ben Azzai says: He recites four prayers, two upon his entrance and two upon his exit. In addition to praying that he may enter and depart in peace, he gives thanks for the past and cries out in prayer for the future.

mishnayos.summary: We must thank Hashem for bad things just like good things, and we must treat the Beis HaMikdash with great respect. The Sages also made new rules, like greeting people with Hashem's name.

chunks.en: A person must say a bracha on bad things
just like he says a bracha on good things,
as the Torah says (Devarim 6):

words.note: A pasuk number in the Tanach, not read aloud.

chunks.en: You shall love Hashem your God

chunks.he: בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ וּבְכָל נַפְשְׁךָ וּבְכָל מְאֹדֶךָ.
chunks.en: with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might.
"With all your heart" means
with both parts of you that want things,
with the yetzer tov and the yetzer hara.

words.note: The yetzer tov is the part of us that wants to do good; the yetzer hara wants to do wrong.

chunks.en: "And with all your soul" means
even if He takes away your life.
"And with all your might" means
with all your money.
Another way to explain "with all your might":

chunks.he: בְּכָל מִדָּה וּמִדָּה שֶׁהוּא מוֹדֵד לְךָ
chunks.en: whatever way Hashem treats you,
thank Him very, very much.
A person should not act silly or disrespectful
facing the Eastern Gate,

words.note: The Eastern Gate was the main gate in the wall of Har HaBayis.

chunks.he: שֶׁהוּא מְכֻוָּן כְּנֶגֶד בֵּית קָדְשֵׁי הַקָּדָשִׁים.
chunks.en: because it lines up straight with the Holy of Holies.

words.note: The Kodesh HaKodashim was the holiest room in the Beis HaMikdash.

chunks.en: He should not go onto Har HaBayis with his walking stick,

words.note: Har HaBayis is the Temple Mount, where the Beis HaMikdash stood.

chunks.en: or with his shoes, or with his money belt,

words.note: A punda was a hollow belt that people kept money in.

chunks.en: or with dust on his feet,
and he should not use it as a shortcut,
and spitting there is surely forbidden.

words.note: A kal vachomer is a reason that says: if this small thing is not allowed, a bigger thing surely is not.

chunks.en: At the end of all the brachos said in the Beis HaMikdash,
they used to say "forever" (min ha'olam).
Once the heretics went bad

words.note: Minim were Jews who stopped believing in the Torah's true teachings.

chunks.en: and said there is only one world (no Olam Haba),
the Sages made a rule that people should say
"from this world until the next world."
They also made a rule that a person should ask
how his friend is, using Hashem's name,
as it says (Rus 2):

words.note: A pasuk number in the Tanach, not read aloud.

chunks.en: And here came Boaz from Beis Lechem,

words.note: Boaz was a great leader who married Rus; he was King David's great-grandfather.

chunks.en: and he said to the harvesters, "Hashem is with you,"
and they said to him,
"May Hashem bless you."
And it also says (Shoftim 6):

words.note: A pasuk number in the Tanach, not read aloud.

chunks.en: "Hashem is with you, mighty hero."
And it also says (Mishlei 23):

words.note: A pasuk number in the Tanach, not read aloud.

chunks.en: "Do not look down on your mother when she is old."
And it also says (Tehillim 119):

words.note: A pasuk number in the Tanach, not read aloud.

chunks.en: "It is a time to act for Hashem; they have broken Your Torah."
Rabbi Nasan says:

words.note: A great Rabbi of the Mishnah.

chunks.en: "They broke Your Torah" because "it is a time to act for Hashem."

mishnayos.english: The mishna articulates a general principle: One is obligated to recite a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he recites a blessing for the good that befalls him, as it is stated: “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5). The mishna explains this verse as follows: “With all your heart” means with your two inclinations, with your good inclination and your evil inclination, both of which must be subjugated to the love of God. “With all your soul” means even if God takes your soul. “And with all your might” means with all your money, as money is referred to in the Bible as might. Alternatively, it may be explained that “with all your might” means with every measure that He metes out to you; whether it is good or troublesome, thank Him. The mishna teaches several Temple-related halakhot. One may not act irreverently or conduct himself flippantly opposite the eastern gate of the Temple Mount, which is aligned opposite the Holy of Holies. In deference to the Temple, one may not enter the Temple Mount with his staff, his shoes, his money belt [punda], or even the dust on his feet. One may not make the Temple a shortcut to pass through it, and through an a fortiori inference, all the more so one may not spit on the Temple Mount. The mishna relates: At the conclusion of all blessings recited in the Temple, those reciting the blessing would say: Blessed are You Lord, God of Israel, until everlasting [haolam], the world. But when the Sadducees strayed and declared that there is but one world and there is no World-to-Come, the Sages instituted that at the conclusion of the blessing one recites: From everlasting [haolam] to everlasting [haolam]. The Sages also instituted that one should greet another in the name of God, i.e., one should mention God’s name in his greeting, as it is stated: “And presently Boaz came from Bethlehem and said to the harvesters, The Lord is with you, and they said to him, May the Lord bless you” (Ruth 2:4). And it says: “And the angel of God appeared to him and said to him, God is with you, mighty man of valor” (Judges 6:12). And it says: “And despise not your mother when she is old” (Proverbs 23:22), i.e., one must not neglect customs which he inherits. And lest you say that mentioning God’s name is prohibited, it says: “It is time to work for the Lord; they have made void Your Torah” (Psalms 119:126), i.e., it is occasionally necessary to negate biblical precepts in order to perform God’s will, and greeting another is certainly God’s will. Rabbi Natan says another interpretation of the verse: “Make void Your Torah” because “it is the time to work for the Lord,” i.e., occasionally it is necessary to negate biblical precepts in order to bolster the Torah.
